earlier_scan.note: ANU repository bitstream link redirects to a migration page; Aeka otherwise treated as Orokaiva dialect with no separate phonology found.

sources.citation: Smallhorn, Jacinta M. 2011. The Binanderean languages of Papua New Guinea: reconstruction and subgrouping. Pacific Linguistics 625. Canberra: ANU (PhD ANU 2009).
sources.note: Sec. 3.6 Suprasegmentals pp.79-80 (PDF 95-96): penultimate stress 'assumed' for Proto Binandere 2-3-syllable non-verbs because 'Suena, Zia, Binandere, Hunjara, Tafota Baruga, and Korafe all exhibit this pattern' -- Aeka not named; no Aeka-specific stress statement anywhere. p.15: Aeka data = wordlists only (Chinnery & Beaver 1915 'Aiga'; Wilson 1969a 35 words; Farr & Larsen 1979 c.100 words). p.47: 'The speakers themselves generally consider Aeka (or Northern Orokaiva) and Hunjara (or Mountain Orokaiva) to be separate languages'. Of 267 Aeka cognate-set rows only 2 carry a stress mark (ti'ŋge…

sources.citation: Larsen, Robert & Marlys Larsen. 1982 [1985]. Orokaiva legends, lessons and grammar notes (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 30). Ukarumpa: SIL. (Rosetta Project excerpt)
sources.note: Grammar Notes p.77 sec. 1.3: 'In Orokaiva words, the first syllable is the most stressed.. The second greatest emphasis is on the third syllable in words longer than two syllables.' Lessons p.64: words are 'in the Sose or Central Orokaiva dialect'. Not Aeka.

sources.citation: Larsen, Robert & Marlys Larsen. 1977. Orokaiva phonology and orthography. In R. Loving (ed.), Phonologies of five P.N.G. languages (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 19), 5-28. Ukarumpa: SIL.
sources.note: p.12 sec. 5.1: 'Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word.' But p.5: 'The dialect studied was that spoken by the people who live between Agenehambo and Wasida on the road from Popondetta to Kokoda' = Orokaiva proper, not Aeka.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record aeka1244; transnewguinea.org / Lexibank Aeka wordlist pages.
sources.note: Glottolog: most extensive description = Chinnery & Beaver 1915 wordlist; 0 descriptive refs. transnewguinea.org Aeka words are drawn from Smallhorn 2011, Wilson 1969 and McElhanon & Voorhoeve 1970; no stress marks.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Aeka language' (redirects to Orokaiva language article).
sources.note: Phonology given is Orokaiva's (citing Larsen & Larsen 1977), not Aeka-specific.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2017. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics 4), 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. (Binanderean source census, p.52)
sources.note: Nothing; it certifies (as of 2017, by Hammarström's own bibliography) that the best sources for Aeka are two comparative overviews, i.e. no grammar, sketch or phonology exists for Aeka, while Orokaiva proper has three sketches.

sources.note: Sole resource listed for Aeka: 'RETSEMA, Thom, researcher; GEORGE Western Gariapa; TUTEPA, Bonny, speakers. 2006. Aeka [aez] Word List, Kikinonda village.' (show_work.asp?id=928474542177). No phonology, no grammar. The work page/PDF has no archived copy at the Internet Archive (CDX = []).

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald & Sebastian Nordhoff. 2012. Online appendix to 'The languages of Melanesia: quantifying the level of coverage'. In N. Evans & M. Klamer (eds), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia (LD&C Special Publication 5), 13-34. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: coverage inventory only: entry lists only Dutton 1975b and Wilson 1969a [overview, comparative]; no phonology; no stress/tone statement (database of descriptive coverage, not a description)

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2007. Change Request 2007-190 (submitted by Rachel Hiley, SIL PNG): split [ork] Orokaiva into [okv], [hkk] Hunjara-Kaina Ke, [aez] Aeka; adopted 2008-01-14.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Identity: 'Aeka is 72% lexically similar to Orokaiva. However, Aeka speakers consider their language as different from Orokaiva. They reported very low comprehension of Orokaiva' (p.2); based on a 7-day SIL survey in the Aeka area.

sources.note: bibliography only: index lists only Chinnery & Beaver 1917 and Capell 1962; no phonology manuscript recorded

sources.citation: Dutton, T. E. 1975. South-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 613-664.
sources.note: Sec. 2.9.5.8.3.2 p.647: Aeka 'spoken in a collection of villages along the middle and lower reaches of the Opi and Kumusi Rivers'; pop. 2000?. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Larsen, Robert. 1975. Difference coefficients for determining dialect relatedness. MA thesis, University of North Dakota (Grand Forks).
sources.note: Comparative phonological study of the Orokaiva dialect chain (per Smallhorn 2011 p.47); may include Northern Orokaiva (= Aeka) villages and any stress differences along the chain.

sources.citation: Healey, Alan, Ambrose Isoroembo & Martin Chittleborough. 1969. Preliminary notes on Orokaiva grammar. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 9 (Pacific Linguistics A-18), 33-64.
sources.note: p.34: 'The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed.' Orokaiva proper; Aeka not mentioned.

sources.citation: Wilson, Darryl. 1969. The Binandere language family. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 9 (Pacific Linguistics A-18), 65-86.
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 pp.68-69, 'based mainly on the six northern members of the family' (Aeka is southern): only 'tone is separate from stress and may well be phonemic' for Suena. Aeka appears only in the village list (p.67) and the 35-item wordlist (pp.80-81, no stress marks). No Aeka stress statement.
